lines: Before it was a relic, it was news. And news needed a printer.
Benjamin Franklin knew the power of print long before he helped shape the Declaration.
Thomas Jefferson drafted the words. His colleagues and Congress revised them.
On the night of July fourth, seventeen seventy-six, John Dunlap's shop set the Declaration in type.
Copies traveled. On July ninth, Washington had the Declaration read to his troops in New York.
A decade later, Hamilton, Madison, and Jay used print to argue for the Constitution as Publius.
Different hands. Different roles. One enduring idea: public words must reach the public. We carry that conviction onto our press in Austin.
Read the words. Keep the source. Make your own first impression.
